[
377
]

The correspondence dated September 11, 2018,
authored by Ms. Saad of the Sexual Assault Crisis Centre, is also admitted.
The correspondence evidences developments that have occurred since the trial
concerning the appellant’s participation in four counselling sessions beginning
in July 2018 and the offer that was made by Ms. Saad to the appellant, to refer
her to “SACC Groups” for further therapeutic benefit.  Again, in the context of
the totality of the available evidence, little weight is afforded to the
content of this documentation.

[
378
]

As with other documents, this correspondence
only provides information of a general nature.  Further, Ms. Saad’s expresses
an opinion that the appellant understands how her “
past conduct
” may
have negatively affected her children.  Ms. Saad does not identify the specific
nature of the potential harm to which she speaks, nor the particulars of the
appellant’s
past conduct
to which she refers.  Further, the
correspondence indicates that the appellant disclosed that her “
past conduct
”
was based on “
behaviours that were normalized
” as she grew up, without
specifying the nature of the past conduct to which the appellant is said to
have referred.

[
379
]

Given the nature of the protection findings made
by the trial judge, it was essential that the appellant’s past conduct that
forms the basis of the foregoing aspects of Ms. Saad’s correspondence be expressly
identified.  In the absence of such evidence, the court is not in a position to
determine whether the appellant’s “
past conduct
” that was normalized by
the circumstances of her upbringing, includes and/or is limited to the
circumstances surrounding the cell phone video that formed the basis of the
appellant’s criminal convictions or whether there are other undisclosed aspects
of the appellant’s “
past conduct
”, to which Ms. Saad and the appellant
refer.

[
380
]

The correspondence dated September 10, 2018 (or
October 9, 2018), authored by Becky Swift of the Canadian Mental Health
Association is admissible.  In a general manner, that correspondence primarily
describes the appellant’s post-trial involvement with the CMHA Justice Program,
which began in June 2018.  Again, considered in the context of the evidence as
a whole, the content of this document attracts little evidentiary weight.

[
381
]

Although Ms. Swift records that the appellant’s
most recent OCAN shows that the appellant has “
demonstrated insight
pertaining to her diagnosis and symptoms
”, neither an actual specified
diagnosis nor the nature and extent of the appellant’s symptoms are, in fact,
disclosed.  This is a deficit that cuts through a substantial amount of the
evidence that the appellant seeks to adduce on appeal.  Despite the appellant’s
continuing involvement with a psychiatrist since 2013 and her engagement with
several forms of counselling, post-trial, (which forms the subject matter of
aspects of her own affidavit evidence together with exhibits appended thereto),
there is no evidence that establishes an actual mental health diagnosis or
prognosis with respect to the appellant.  Such evidence is essential in order
to allow the court to place the appellant’s evidence and related exhibits in
appropriate context.  Such evidence is notoriously absent.

[
382
]

Turning to the balance of the exhibits appended
to the appellant’s affidavit, I decline to admit as evidence on appeal, the
certificates related to the appellant’s pre-trial participation in the “Strong
Women Circle”; the “Taking Charge Program”; and the “Women’s Empowerment
Program”.  These certificates were put before the trial judge who explained in
detail, both during the course of the trial and in his reasons, the
deficiencies associated with this evidence as it relates to the determination
of the disposition that is consistent with the children’s best interests.  It
is clear that the trial judge had regard to the appellant’s stated
participation in these programs in arriving at his disposition, because the
appellant provided
viva voce
evidence at trial in that regard.  The
certificates themselves, which the appellant now seeks to adduce again on
appeal, do not probatively add to the evidentiary base that was before the
trial judge.  Recall, the issue the trial judge had with the certificates was
not whether or not the appellant “participated” in the identified programs but
the nature and extent of her participation and the potential insight gained
therefrom.  The certificates do not assist in the determination of those
matters.  For the reasons expressed by the trial judge (and summarized earlier
in these reasons), which I adopt, I arrive at the same conclusion.

[
383
]

The documentary evidence from St. Clair College
concerning the appellant’s post-trial educational pursuits is admitted.  In my
view, that documentation potentially informs the appellant’s long term ability
to provide for the children’s needs, at least from a financial perspective.

[
384
]

The affidavit of Ms. Market is also admitted
subject to paragraph 9, in which she deposes “I see [C.W.]’s progress as proof
she has gained insight into her life and lifestyle.”  That statement is an
inadmissible opinion.  Ms. Market did not deliver a
curriculum vitae
nor
was a request made to have her qualified as an expert (or recognized as a
participant expert) for the purpose of offering opinion evidence to the court.

[
385
]

S.H.’s affidavit evidence is also admitted as it
relates to post-trial developments related to the circumstances of the
appellant (at least in the period from October 1, 2018, when S.H. became a
subtenant, to November 5, 2018 when she swore her affidavit).

[
386
]

Finally, I am satisfied that the additional
evidence offered by the Society as set out in paragraphs 1 to 24 of Ms.
Schofield’s affidavit, sworn November 15, 2018, ought to be admitted.  It
satisfies the criteria to be admitted as further or fresh evidence on appeal
and it contextually informs the additional evidence adduced by the appellant.
There are aspects of the content of Ms. Schofield’s affidavit set out in
paragraphs 25 to 36, in which she generally purports to respond to the
appellant’s affidavit sworn November 5, 2018, which require further consideration.
I find the content of those paragraphs to be admissible subject to the
following:

(a)        Paragraph 28 – the second sentence and last sentence of
paragraph 28 are only admissible as evidence of Ms. Schofield’s view of the
children’s continuing need for protection in her capacity as a family services
worker.

(b)        Paragraph 29 – the entirety of the paragraph is only
admissible as evidence of Ms. Schofield’s belief in the children’s continuing
need for protection.  Apart from that issue, the content of paragraph 29
constitutes argument.

Impact of
the Fresh and Further Evidence

[
387
]

I am not persuaded that the fresh and further
evidence adduced by the parties warrants this court interfering with the trial
judge’s disposition nor does it warrant a new trial.  I will explain.

[
388
]

The circumstances disclosed by the fresh
evidence are generally consistent with the prevailing circumstances and factual
matrix that were operable at the time of trial.

[
389
]

The additional evidence admitted on appeal is
consistent with the trial judge’s finding that the subject children have a
connection with the EWMNNS, which was a factor of which he remained mindful
when considering the enumerated “best interests” criteria set out in  s. 74(3)
of the
CYFSA
and ultimately, in arriving at his disposition.

[
390
]

The additional evidence on appeal is also
consistent with the evidence developed at trial through Ms. Schofield and Grand
Chief Mary Lou Parker that indicates that the EWMNNS does not offer placements
for children with other Métis families within its community as well as Grand
Chief Mary Lou Parker’s confirmation that no such placements were available for
the children in this instance.  The additional evidence is also consistent with
the trial evidence indicating that the EWMNNS does not offer child-related
services to its members or their respective children.

[
391
]

The appellant’s affidavit evidence generally
suggests that she was more immersed in indigenous cultural activities at the
time of trial than she deposed to at that time, and further that she immersed
the children in Métis culture before apprehension to a greater extent than she
deposed to at trial.  The specific date or dates upon which she began to engage
in cultural activities such as smudging, drumming, and singing are not set out
in her affidavit and remain unclear.

[
392
]

The additional evidence admitted on appeal
confirms that the Society has not ignored the children’s cultural needs while
they have been in Society care.  To the contrary,                   Ms.
Schofield’s affidavit evidence establishes that once the Society was advised of
the children’s connection with the EWMNNS, it undertook continuous efforts to
provide appropriate indigenous services to the children including:  books,
lessons and the involvement of both the Métis Nation of Ontario (something
which the appellant ultimately opposed) and a Family Wellness Worker from the
Can-Am Indian Friendship Centre of Windsor; contacting the EWMNNS to develop
information with respect to the children’s membership in that community and
information concerning services and placement opportunities available through
that community; and providing appropriate education and training to the
children’s foster parents in respect of the children’s cultural needs and Métis
heritage.

[
393
]

Ms. Schofield’s affidavit clearly establishes
that the children have been and continue to be in receipt of specific lessons
with respect to their Métis culture and heritage.  Further, the appellant,
herself, has long been aware of the Society’s efforts in that regard.  Ms.
Schofield deposes that post-apprehension, the appellant herself was referred by
the Society to the Métis Nation of Ontario (a Métis community with which she
ultimately did not want to work).  The Society experienced difficulty obtaining
specific information relative to the children’s Métis heritage from the
appellant.  Indeed, when Ms. Schofield originally became involved with the
family, the appellant was unable to provide her with any information concerning
the EWMNNS.  Subsequently, the appellant was unable to provide contact
information for Grand Chief Mary Lou Parker and the appellant did not describe
a familiarity with the EWMNNS community.

[
394
]

Ms. Schofield deposes that as of March 5, 2018,
(approximately two months before trial) the appellant confirmed that she had
not had any contact with the EWMNNS and she was unable to provide any details
of cultural services either she or her children had engaged in within Ontario.
The appellant provided a release, dated February 15, 2018, to the Society
permitting a referral to be made on behalf of the children to a Family Wellness
Worker at the Can-An Indian Friendship Centre.  The referral was made the
following day and cultural programming and community services were arranged
through that organization for both the children and the children’s foster
parents.

[
395
]

Ms. Schofield also deposes that at a plan of
care meeting on May 28, 2018, for which the appellant was present the Can-Am
Indian Friendship Centre Family Wellness Worker provided an update with respect
to the cultural services being provided to the children and also recommended
that the children engage in services through the Métis Nation of Ontario.  The
appellant did not provide any suggestions of her own regarding instruction or
cultural services for the children or their foster parents.

[
396
]

Notably, the appellant has
not
sought to
adduced any evidence denying the foregoing aspects of Ms. Schofield’s evidence,
even though she has delivered evidence in which she specifically denies other
aspects of Ms. Schofield’s affidavit evidence.  The foregoing aspects of the
Society’s additional evidence on appeal demonstrate that the Society has
engaged in meaningful efforts to ensure that the children’s cultural traditions
and heritage are respected and that their cultural needs are met through the
provision of direct services both by and through Society Family Service Worker,
Ms. Rusenstrom, and the Can-Am Indian Friendship Centre of Windsor Family
Wellness Worker, Ms. Robinson, and by ensuring that the children’s foster
parents had appropriate cultural education and training.  That evidence is not
contradicted by trial evidence or the fresh and further evidence adduced by the
appellant.

[
397
]

The documentary evidence adduced by the appellant
suggests that she first sought services related to the children through the
Can-Am Indian Friendship Centre of Windsor on November 15, 2017, which was
almost a year and a half after the children were placed in the continuous care
of the Society and nearly half a year after the four month Society wardship
imposed by Ross J. ended.  Yet she did not commence participation in the
Bringing Home Tradition Parenting program until after the trial.

[
398
]

The appellant’s fresh evidence with respect to
her ongoing efforts:  to gain further insight and skills in order to mitigate
the risks that led to the protection findings made by the trial judge; to
receive counselling for her multi-faceted issues (from a variety of service
providers) and her immersion in daily indigenous activities, traditions and
teachings (including interacting with elders) is generally consistent with the
nature of the evidence that she gave in that regard at trial, albeit in more
detail.  The additional evidence on appeal does not disclose that the appellant
has any greater appreciation of the children’s developmental needs as deposed
to by Ms. Rusenstrom (at trial) than the level of appreciation disclosed by the
appellant’s trial evidence.  The appellant’s limited plan in that regard, as
she expressed it at trial, remains the same.

[
399
]

The appellant’s post-trial efforts to improve
herself and her life circumstances are all commendable.  However, her efforts
in that regard do not appreciably alter the factual matrix that was before the
trial judge to an extent that would justify a different disposition than the
one he arrived at or, alternatively, that would warrant a new trial.  I will
explain.

[
400
]

The additional evidence on appeal concerning the
appellant’s post-trial self-improvement efforts must be evaluated in context.
Specifically, the children came into the continuous care of the Society in
July, 2016.  As a result, at the time of appeal, the oldest child had spent
nearly 45 percent of her life in continuous Society care and the youngest child
has spent nearly 70 percent of his life in continuous Society care.  Both s. 70
of the
CFSA
(legislation which governed almost the entirety of the
pre-trial time period in this proceeding) and
s. 122
of the
CYFSA
,
provide that children under the age of six years old cannot spend more than 12
months in temporary Society care.  That time limit was markedly exceeded well
before the trial of the status review application took place.  The actions that
were taken (and not taken) by the appellant during that time to address the
circumstances that gave rise to the protection findings in this proceeding are
relevant.

[
401
]

In May, 2016, Ross J. made a temporary order
placing the children in the appellant’s care subject to supervision, on terms.
The appellant breached one of those terms within approximately two months of
the order being made.  Her non-compliance resulted in the removal of the
children from her care.  Ross J. then made the original protection finding on
February 1, 2017 and endorsed a plan of care that required the appellant to
participate in and complete certain programs and services within a four month
period.  As the trial evidence reveals, the appellant did not fully comply with
those terms.  The Society also specified a plan of care in May, 2017 that
required the appellant to engage in certain programs and services.  The
appellant did not fully comply with the terms of that plan of care prior to the
trial of the status review application in May, 2018.

[
402
]

Further, the appellant
conceded
at the
trial of the status review application that the evidence supported a finding
that the children would continue to be in need of protection from exposure to
adult domestic violence in the event that they were returned to her care at
that time.  Contextually, that concession was made:  two years after Ross J.’s
temporary order; almost two years after the children were removed from the
appellant’s care in July 2016; approximately one and a quarter years after Ross
J.’s original protection finding; and after the appellant failed to fully
achieve the objectives of two successive plans of care on a timely basis, or at
all.  Thus, despite the passage of a substantial amount of time and ongoing
identification of required services and objectives, by her own admissions, the
children were still at risk of harm in her care in May 2018.

[
403
]

Finally, despite the appellant’s evidence
concerning her improved insight into the risks of harm posed by her past
conduct, including those related to domestic violence, it remains that the
appellant, under oath, denied any incident of domestic violence between herself
and T.E. at trial.  Notably, she did
not
expressly resile from that
aspect of her evidence through the additional evidence she adduced on appeal.
This results in a paradox in which the appellant’s evidence, taken in its
totality, indicates she has gained insight into historic domestic violence
issues with T.E. that never existed, in fact.  All of the foregoing illuminates
the context in which the additional evidence about the appellant’s post-trial
efforts to improve herself and to address the identified protection concerns,
must be evaluated.

[
404
]

Since the conclusion of the trial, the appellant
appears to have engaged in earnest efforts to access services and programming
that she could have accessed prior to trial.  However, the evidence also reveals
that the appellant’s post-trial service providers have made recommendations for
further services, including through the Hiatus House and the Sexual Assault
Crisis Centre’s “groups”, which the appellant has not yet accessed or pursued.
To be clear, the appellant’s efforts directed at self-improvement are salutary,
but the children cannot be parked in limbo while the appellant attempts to
straighten out her life:  see
Children’s Aid Society of Waterloo v. V.
L.
,

2007 ONCA 113
, at paras.
13-14
.  Time is an important consideration under the
CYFSA
.
The appellant was afforded a significant amount of time prior to trial (i.e.
two years) to take the necessary steps to adequately mitigate the protection
risks that are operable in this instance.  She did not do so.

[
405
]

When considered together, the additional
evidence adduced from the appellant’s post-trial service providers in the form
of brief correspondence and the appellant’s own affidavit do not amount to
compelling evidence of a substantial post-trial change in the circumstances
related to the risks of harm that would be posed to the children by their
return to the appellant’s care, as found by the trial judge.  In that regard,
the appellant’s own additional affidavit evidence on appeal with respect to her
insight into the issues associated with her
past conduct
(in relation to
domestic abuse and the circumstances surrounding the video recording) is
essentially a restatement of the evidence that she gave at trial.  That
evidence was considered and reasonably rejected by the trial judge.  The
balance of the evidence admitted on appeal does not demonstrate a marked
improvement in that regard.  I have already explained my reasons for concluding
that little weight attaches to the content of the correspondence from the
appellant’s service providers, which is appended to her affidavit.  Finally,
the other evidence concerning the appellant’s post-trial partner choice (or
choices) militates against the appellant’s remedial request on appeal.  I will
explain.

[
406
]

There is equivocation in the record as to
whether the appellant has, in fact, associated with T.E. post-trial and whether
there have been further incidents of domestic violence between them.  The
Society received disclosure from M.G. in that regard, which does not appear to
be verified.  Conversely, the appellant testifies that M.G. is untruthful and
her false reports are motivated by revenge.  Curiously, however, when she was
first advised about M.G.’s allegations by Ms. Schofield, the appellant
indicated that she was not aware of any reason why M.G. would fabricate such
things.  Further, the appellant does not explain how M.G. would even have known
about T.E. and the appellant’s past relationship with him, in the absence of
T.E. associating with the appellant post-trial, particularly since M.G. only
started living with the appellant in June, 2018 (i.e. after the trial had
concluded) and the appellant maintains that she last associated with T.E. in
July 2016.

[
407
]

More fundamentally, the appellant’s history with
C.M. raises concerns with respect to the appellant’s ability to avoid abusive
relationships.  The appellant acknowledges that she engaged in a relationship
with C.M. despite her characterization of him as:  a controlling personality
who was jealous and demanding; and a person who would periodically take her
cell phone and refuse to return it.  The appellant acknowledged that she did
not feel safe with C.M. when he took her cell phone.  She felt it was necessary
to involve police to attend C.M.’s home to retrieve it.

[
408
]

Then the police were called a second time, three
weeks later, because notwithstanding her stated concerns over C.M.’s behaviour,
the appellant returned to his residence as a consequence of his stated desire
to reconcile with her.  Once there, according to the appellant, C.M. threatened
physical violence against her.  The appellant’s willingness to reconcile with
C.M., after he engaged in the behaviour that she describes and after her
perceived need to involve the services of police in their fledgling relationship,
causes concern that she has not developed adequate insight into the risks of
harm posed by her involvement in abusive relationships.

[
409
]

The additional evidence on appeal does not
displace the evidence before the trial judge that:  a significant risk of harm
to the children would arise if the they were returned to the appellant’s care;
the children had substantial developmental needs when they came into Society
care in July, 2016, which had not been previously addressed by the appellant;
the children’s developmental needs have been and continue to be addressed
through services engaged by the Society and through the efforts of the
children’s foster parents; all of the children’s needs are currently being met
in stable environments in which they have existed since July 2016; a foster
parent wants to adopt both children subject to no access or photograph access;
and the children are currently safe.

[
410
]

The children are Métis.  The additional evidence
on appeal demonstrates that the Society has arranged for and provided services
to preserve and advance the children’s cultural identities and their connection
with their Métis culture and heritage.  The Society has also arranged for
services for the foster parents and direct assistance to the children’s foster
parents (including the proposed adoptive parent), in order to educate and train
them to support the preservation and furtherance of the children’s cultural
identities.

[
411
]

The additional evidence does not displace the
evidence before the trial judge that demonstrated that placing the children
with their maternal grandmother in Nova Scotia is not consistent with their
best interests.  The only additional evidence on appeal concerning the merits
of such a placement is that the appellant no longer associates with C.W.  The
additional evidence does not disclose any other potential community placements
for the children, including a placement with a Métis family.

[
412
]

Finally, the trial judge’s findings and
disposition were made after a careful and reasoned determination of the
credibility of the appellant and the reliability of her evidence, which
resulted in a stated diminishment of the extent to which the trial judge could
rely on those aspects of her evidence that he did not otherwise expressly
reject.  In my view, when considered in its totality, the additional evidence
and information on appeal does not operate to disturb the basis of those
findings nor the basis for the factual findings upon which the trial judge
determined the children’s best interests and disposition, to an extent that
would justify this court substituting a different disposition for that of the
trial judge, or ordering a new trial as the appellant seeks.

CONCLUSION

[
413
]

For the foregoing reasons, I do not give effect
to any of the argued grounds for appeal.  The fresh and further evidence
admitted on appeal does not change the underlying factual matrix presented by
the evidence at trial to such an extent that it warrants substituting a
different disposition for that of the trial judge or ordering a new trial, as
the appellant requests.

[
414
]

As a result of the foregoing, the appeal is
dismissed.
